CASE REPORT

Ivanka Marinović1, Dinko Pivalica1, Jure Aljinović1, Tonko Vlak1, Ela Škorić1 and Dušanka Martinović Kaliterna2
1Department of Rehabilitation Medicine and Rheumatology, University Hospital Split, School of Medicine in Split, Split, Croatia
and 2Department of Rheumatology and Clinical Immunology, University Hospital Split, School of Medicine in Split, Split, Croatia
Abstract
Keywords

Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by
progressive stiffness and rigidity of truncal muscles accompanied with co-contraction of
agonist–antagonist muscles. Our 51-year-old female patient was presented for the first time
to physiatrists in 2006 and diagnosed with axial-spondyloarthropathy (SpA) HLA-B27 positive.
SPS was diagnosed 7 years after initial symptoms. SPS should be taken into consideration
in HLA-B27 positive patients if stiffness of paravertebral and abdominal muscles progresses
during SpA therapy.

Anti-GAD, HLA-B27, Spondyloarthropathy,
Stiff Person Syndrome, Truncal rigidity

Introduction
Case report

Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune neurological
disorder. It is characterized by progressive stiffness and rigidity,
prominence of truncal muscles accompanied with co-contraction
of agonist and antagonist muscles. In patients suffering from SPS,
sudden episodic spasms are precipitated by unexpected tactile,
audio, visual, and emotional stimuli [1, 2]. Progressive muscle
stiffness and rigidity, superimposed by spasms, results in postural
deformities, difficulties at bending and turning and slow, deliberate, and wide gait.
Many patients suffering from SPS also have insulindependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM) (30%), autoimmune thyroiditis (10%) and/or pernicious anemia (5%). In most cases,
SPS is an idiopathic condition. Nevertheless, in 5% of patients
SPS appears as a paraneoplastic manifestation. These patients
usually have more prominent stiffness in the neck and arms
[2, 3]. Auto-antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD), the rate-limiting enzyme necessary for synthesis of
gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), are present in 80% of all
patients [4, 5]. This syndrome affects both sexes but there are
more reports of affected woman. SPS tends to occur in the
fourth to sixth decade of life [6].
Diagnosis essentially relies on clinical observation, and is confirmed by detection of anti-GAD in the serum and by characteristic
electromyography (EMG) abnormalities, all included in Dalakas
criteria used worldwide [6].
Here we would like to report a clinical case of a woman suffering from SPS whose diagnostic procedure took 7 years due to
clinical resemblance of SPS with HLA-B27 positive axial spondyloarthropathy (SpA).

A 51-year-old woman presented for the first time to the physiatrist in the Department of Physical Medicine, Rehabilitation and
Rheumatology of University Hospital Centre Split, in November
of 2006. She was suffering severe pain in the lumbar region and
moderate pain in the cervical region of the spine. During physical
examination her cervical and lumbar paravertebral muscles were
painful and rigid. The limitations of the movements in the lumbar
and cervical regions were noted. Plain radiographs of the cervical
and lumbar spine, as well as computed tomography of the lumbar
spine showed mild degenerative changes. The patient received
ibuprofen (1200–1600 mg/day), during 1-month period.
At that time, she was prescribed periodical intensive physical
therapy that included exercises of stretching and relaxation of the
spine muscles, mobilization of the lumbar and cervical spine, thermotherapy and hydrotherapy until April 2008. Performed physical therapy showed some success. The patient still presented an
inflammatory back pain in the lumbar spine including morning
stiffness lasting up to 2 hours that tended to improve after exercise
and frequent nocturnal awakenings.
Anamnesis revealed that patient’s initial symptoms began in
her 40s and included pain and morning stiffness of the cervical
and lumbar spine and unilateral heel pain. Her father had ankylosing spondylitis (AS), HLA-B27 positive. No clinical evidence or
anamnestic data of psoriatic changes of the skin, genitourinary,
gastrointestinal, and ocular infections were obtained. Physical
examination of patient revealed loss of cervical and lumbar lordosis and pain and rigidity of cervical and lumbar paravertebral
muscles. The range of spinal movements was reduced: modified
Schober’s test 2 cm, chest expansion 1. 5 cm, lumbar lateral bending 67 cm (distance between the tip of the third finger and the
floor). Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) was calculated to be 5. 3 and Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis
Functional Index (BASFI) scores was 8. 7. In laboratory findings

spondyloarthropathy HLA-B27 positive and Stiff Person
Syndrome – rheumatologist point of view

A laboratory measurement of the anti-GAD antibody in serum was
167 U/mL (normal range 0–0. 9 U/mL). EMG showed a continuous
motor unit activity of both agonist and antagonist muscles at the
same time. Patient fulfilled Dalakas criteria for the diagnoses of
typical SPS [6].

Discussion
This is a case report of extremely rare coincidence of nonradiographic axial SpA HLA-B27 positive and typical form of
SPS. To the best of our knowledge this is the first description of
this coincidence. In this patient axial SpA was diagnosed early
after the first clinical manifestations, while SPS was diagnosed
7 years after her first examination in our department, due to
clinical resemblance with HLA-B27 positive axial SpA. Furthermore, the variability in clinical presentation of SPS is the
main reason why it is usually misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed.
According to Dalakas, delay in diagnosis ranges from 1 to 18
years, with a mean of 6. 2 years [6]. Also, axial SpA tends to
show slow progression and it often takes years to decades of
clinical symptoms to develop radiographic manifestation [7].
The main problem for all of the physicians that examined the
patient was fixation on axial SpA.
In our patient, SpA or probable AS were always noted as a work
diagnosis. Furthermore, the patient fulfilled the ESSG criterion for
SpA due to inflammatory spinal pain, positive family history and
enthesopathy. She had also fulfilled AMOR SpA classification
criteria due to lumbar pain during the night and morning stiffness
of lumbar region, heel pain, HLA-B27, positive family history of
AS, clear general improvement and rapid relapse of the pain after
non-steroid anti inflammatory drugs (NSAID) intake.
According to modified New York classification, our patient had
three positive clinical criteria. Due to lack of radiological evidence
of sacroiliitis only probable diagnosis of AS could be concluded.
The reason is that modified New York classification criterion
greatly depends on the radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis.
It is harder to make the diagnosis of AS in women because they
often present in atypical fashion [8]. Women have more pain in the
cervical spine than men, higher burden of disease and less improvement in AS outcome measures compared to men [9]. The data
from the prospective study of outcomes in ankylosing spondylitis
(PSOAS) cohort study revealed that women with AS tend to have
less radiographic spinal damage compared to men [10]. Radiographic damage does not correlate with functional impairment in
both men and women. Moreover, women report more functional
limitation than men at the same level of radiographic damage [8].
In our patient, despite the treatment of axial symptoms,
the disease progressed with increased spasm of paravertebral
muscles and appearance of spasm of the abdominal muscles,
and occasional cramps in the legs. For that reason, we thought
of SPS as a possible concomitant diagnosis and the diagnosis
was confirmed after series of diagnostic procedures proposed
by Dalakas’s criteria. Dalakas criteria include stiffness in the
axial muscles, prominently in the abdominal and thoracolumbar
paravertebral muscles, superimposed painful spasms precipitated
by unexpected noises, emotional stress and tactile stimuli, confirmation of the continuous motor unit activity in agonist and
antagonist muscles by EMG, absence of neurological or cognitive impairments that could explain the stiffness and positive
serology for GAD 65 autoantibody. Response to diazepam is not
a part of Dalakas criteria, but it is commonly included in the
diagnostic criteria [2].
Although SPS is not a common condition, it should be taken
into consideration even in HLA-B27 positive patients if stiffness
of paravertebral and abdominal muscles progresses during SpA

hemogram, routine biochemical analysis, acute phase reactants,
and tumor markers were all within normal range. The results of
the immunological tests including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, C3 and C4
complement protein, antithyreoglobulin antibodies were negative.
The results of urine culture, stool culture, urogenital swab, and
serology of hepatitis were negative. HLA typization showed A1/3,
B27/44; Bw4, and Cw2 genotype. Radiography of the sacroiliac
(SI) joints showed sings of bilateral sacroiliitis, while magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) of the SI joints did not confirm the previous findings. MRI studies of the lumbar, thoracic, and cervical
spine excluded myelopathy and typical radiographic features of
SpA. Scintigraphy of the skeleton with technecium-99 m diphosponate showed accumulation of signal in the corpuses of second,
third, fourth, and fifth lumbar vertebrae. Radiologist from the University Hospital Center Zagreb was consulted and concluded that
this was the case of advanced osteoarthritis of SI joints, without
signs of inflammatory axial disease.
However, we concluded that this was the case of axial SpA
because the patient fulfilled the European Spondyloarthritides
Study Group (ESSG) and AMOR SpA classification criteria for
SpA.
The patient was prescribed indomethacin (150 mg/day) for
2 months that rapidly reduced the pain, but it did not help with the
stiffness. A partial relief of stiffness and rigidity occurred during
physical therapy and consumption of diazepam (4–6 mg/day).
In the second half of the 2008, patient’s clinical condition
worsened and a constant spasm of paravertebral muscles occurred.
Spasms were accompanied by rigidity of abdominal muscles causing detectable inclination of the spine. Patient, who already had
limitations in the everyday activities, started to feel imbalance
due to change of the posture. This resulted with three falls, two
of which ended up with nasal bones’ fractures. After the patient
complained on everyday chest pain with deep breathing, the internal medicine specialist was consulted and excluded rare but severe
cardiopulmonary manifestations of SpA. Other rheumatologists
were consulted and they confirmed the working diagnosis.
From December 2008 to December 2009, the patient was
treated with sulfasalazine (2000–3000 mg/day) but this therapy
was ceased because of ineffectiveness. In March 2010 patient
repeated MRI of SI joints, lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine and
no progression of degenerative changes, nor new signs of inflammatory disease could be seen. The patient’s condition in the year
2010 was complicated by occasional spasms in the muscles of both
legs. The neurologist made comprehensive neurological examination and excluded pyramidal and extrapyramidal disorders.
In the beginning of 2011 a biological therapy for SpA was
taken into consideration. Interferon Gamma Release Assays for
the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infection and Cyfra 21-1 tumor
marker were positive. A blood glucose level was elevated. Extensive pulmonary examination revealed no pathological substrate.
Repeated testing of Cyfra 21-1 was performed and Cyfra 21-1 was
in the normal range. Endocrinologist detected IDDM and excluded
other endocrinology and metabolic diseases. These findings and
patient’s discomfort were the reason why she was not included in
biological therapy.
At that time the patient was taking meloksikam (15 mg/day)

and attended physical therapy periodically. However, the rigidity
of whole spine, especially lumbar segment and abdominal muscles, as well as reduction in movements of cervical spine were still
present. Due to limitation in everyday functioning the patient still
needed constant help to perform everyday activities.
In the beginning of 2013 a rheumatologist at a Department of
Physical Medicine, Rehabilitation and Rheumatology of University Hospital Centre Split suspected that this was the case of SPS.

therapy. It is not usual diagnostic procedure to do EMG of paravertebral muscles and anti-GAD antibody in patients with axial
SpA. In rare cases of progressive rigidity of paravertebral muscles
that looks like tetanus disease, EMG and anti-GAD antibody
should be standardized diagnostic procedures. In conclusion, from
today’s point of view, first symptoms of SPS, including rigidity
of abdominal muscles, loss of balance and falls occurred at the
end of 2008. The typical clinical signs of SPS include stiffness
and rigidity of abdominal and paravertebral muscles as well as an
increase of lumbar lordosis. However, caution should be taken in
differential diagnosis between SPS and SpA, whose typical clinical signs resemble to signs of SPS. Still, the most different point
of SpA from SPS is lack of stiffness and rigidity of abdominal
muscles and loss of lumbar lordosis. To the best of our knowledge
there is no mention of typical form of SPS in differential diagnosis
of axial SpA in the literature.
The aim of this report is to sensitize the medical community to
the possible concomitant existence of this disease in SpA, and its
serious effects on quality of life in affected individual.
